recipe.history:
Chili con carne is one of the most distinctly American dishes in existence, despite the name's Spanish origins and the long-running argument over whether Texas or Mexico deserves credit for its invention. The dish — a spiced beef stew built on chili peppers, cumin, and garlic — almost certainly originated in the cattle trails and border towns of nineteenth-century Texas, where it was developed by tejano and Mexican cooks working with available ingredients: dried chili peppers from the Southwest, tough beef that benefited from long, slow simmering, and the aromatic backbone of cumin, which the Spanish had brought from the Old World. The San Antonio 'chili queens' — women who sold chili from street stands in the city's Military Plaza from the 1860s through the early twentieth century — are often credited with bringing chili to national attention when American tourists and journalists tasted it and brought the news back to their home cities. Philadelphia's food culture, meanwhile, is defined by a very different but equally fierce tradition: the Philly cheesesteak — thin-shaved ribeye, fried onions, and either provolone or Cheese Whiz on an Amoroso roll. Cheese Whiz, the processed cheese sauce developed by Kraft in 1952 and initially marketed for Welsh rarebit, became the definitive authentic cheesesteak topping after Pat Olivieri of Pat's King of Steaks adopted it in the 1950s, and it has remained a point of civic pride in Philadelphia ever since. The CHILI-DELPHIA STORY BURGER fuses these two traditions — Texas chili and Philadelphia cheese culture — in a single, unapologetically indulgent creation.

Chili as a burger topping has deep roots in American diner culture, where the chili burger (or chili size) has been a menu staple since at least the 1930s. California's Tommy's Burgers, founded in 1946, built an empire on a single beef chili poured over burgers; Steak 'n Shake's chili, Bob's Big Boy's chili burger, and the Frito chili pie all belong to the same tradition of piling slow-cooked beef chili onto a patty or into a bun as an act of aggressive generosity. The combination works because chili is itself already a deep, complex beef preparation — its spiced, braised beef deepens and amplifies the seared beef beneath it, a double-beef experience that doubles down rather than diversifies. Cheese Whiz on a burger follows the same logic as Cheese Whiz on a cheesesteak: it provides a smooth, creamy, salty, processed-cheese backbone that flows into every crevice of the chili and the patty, a liquid binding agent that holds the whole construction together while contributing its own specific, unreplicable flavor.

I first made a Philly-style beef chili for a burger on a wet November Saturday when I was thinking about two cities at once. I had a quart of Texas-style beef chili in the refrigerator and a jar of Cheese Whiz in the pantry from a cheesesteak experiment the week before, and the connection seemed almost too obvious to ignore. I heated the chili, thinned the Cheese Whiz slightly with a splash of hot water to make it pourable, cooked a patty to a precise 132 degrees, and poured both over the top in alternating layers. The result was transcendent in the specific way that things you are not supposed to make are always transcendent — rich and impossible and impossible to regret. The chili's spice and the Whiz's saltiness played against the juicy, medium-rare beef the way a horn section plays against a bass line: complementary, reinforcing, and bigger together than either would be alone.

Cooking a burger to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is the absolute prerequisite for a chili burger to succeed. The chili is already rich, already complex, already deeply flavored from its long simmer with chili peppers, cumin, and garlic. The patty must be prepared with equivalent seriousness or it disappears beneath the topping. At 130–135°F, the patty retains enough juice, enough beefy character, and enough textural integrity to hold the structure of the burger together and provide a genuine flavor contribution of its own. The Cheese Whiz is no longer seen as a shortcut when paired with a beautifully medium-rare patty — it is a tradition, a technique, and a testament to the idea that some ingredients earn their place through flavor alone, regardless of their pedigree.
ingredients: kosher salt and black pepper to taste
3–4 tbsp whole milk or hot water (to thin to pourable consistency)
1/2 white onion, finely diced (for topping, Philadelphia-style)
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Whisk warm milk, sugar, and yeast; rest 5 minutes until foamy. Add butter and egg; mix. Add flour and salt; knead 8–10 minutes. Rise in oiled bowl 1 hour. Divide into 4 balls, flatten slightly, proof on parchment 30–40 minutes. Brush with egg wash. Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 15–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on rack.

2. Make the Philly-style beef chili: Heat oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add 450g ground beef and cook, breaking it up with a spoon, until browned and any moisture has evaporated, about 8–10 minutes. Push beef to the side and add diced onion and bell pepper to the pot. Cook 5 minutes until softened. Add garlic; cook 60 seconds.

3. Add chili powder, cumin, smoked paprika, oregano, and cayenne to the pot; stir into the beef and vegetables for 60 seconds, toasting the spices. Add tomato paste; stir and cook 1 minute. Add crushed tomatoes, beef broth, Worcestershire, and apple cider vinegar. Stir to combine, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom of the pot.

4. Bring the chili to a boil, then reduce heat to low. Simmer uncovered for 30–40 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chili has thickened significantly and the flavors have deepened. Season generously with salt and pepper. Taste and adjust spices. Remove from heat and keep warm.

5. Prepare the Cheese Whiz sauce: Place the Cheese Whiz in a small saucepan over very low heat, stirring frequently. Add milk or hot water one tablespoon at a time until the sauce is smooth, warm, and pourable — the consistency of a thick nacho cheese sauce. Do not allow it to scorch. Keep warm over the lowest possible heat.

6. Form the patties: Divide the 700g ground chuck into 4 equal portions (about 175g each). Form into patties 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, pressing a center dimple. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and garlic powder just before cooking.

7. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until very hot. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Sear patties without moving for 3 minutes. Flip once. Cook 2 more minutes. Target internal temperature: 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest 3 minutes off heat.
8. Toast buns cut-side down in the skillet 60–90 seconds until golden.

9. Assemble: Spread yellow mustard on the bottom bun if desired. Place a medium-rare patty on the bottom bun. Spoon 2–3 generous tablespoons of warm Philly beef chili directly over the patty — let it pile up and spill over the sides. Drizzle warm Cheese Whiz over the chili generously. Top with a small mound of finely diced raw white onion — this is traditional Philadelphia style and the sharpness of the raw onion cuts through the richness. Add a few pickle chips. Close carefully with the top bun. Have napkins ready. Serve immediately.
